CHAPTER 12: TESTING AND EVALUATION
12.1 — The Problem: How Do You Measure "Good"?

Imagine an AI product update that scores higher on a general test but now mishandles one task its users rely on—perhaps a support bot that still finds the refund policy but has started responding badly to angry customers. Both results can be true. The general score measures one slice; the failed customer task measures another.

That is the practical problem this chapter solves: what evidence would justify releasing an update for the job people actually need it to do?

Many software tests have an exact expected result: did the calculation return the right number, or did the button complete the intended action? Generative work often adds open-ended qualities. Two explanations can both be factually correct while differing in clarity, tone and usefulness for one reader. The same model may explain one topic well and mishandle your organisation's documents. Evaluation therefore has to define which job and which qualities count—not just ask whether the output exists.

Teams usually combine several kinds of evidence, because each answers a different question:

Public benchmarks — how did the system perform on a shared test of a particular capability?
Human comparison — which response did people prefer under a stated rubric and sample?
Use-case evals — can this exact product still do the tasks and avoid the failures that matter here?

These categories can overlap. A use-case eval may be scored by rules, people, another model or a combination.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Explain what benchmarks are, how they work, and why they exist
Understand why benchmarks are useful but flawed — and what those flaws are
Describe the difference between automated evaluation and human evaluation
Explain what "evals" are in practice and why companies run them constantly
Understand why evaluating generative AI is harder than evaluating traditional software

12.2 — Benchmarks: The Standardised Tests

A benchmark is a shared test used to compare systems on a defined capability. MMLU uses multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects. SWE-bench gives a system a real software issue and checks whether its proposed patch passes repository tests. Other benchmarks use different tasks or human judgments. The score is comparable only when the benchmark version, instructions, tools, settings and scoring method are compatible.

Examples of benchmark families:

BENCHMARK	WHAT IT TESTS	FORMAT
MMLU / MMLU-Pro	General knowledge across 57 subjects	Multiple-choice exam questions
SWE-bench	Real-world coding ability	Gives model actual GitHub bugs; checks if its fix passes the repo's tests
GPQA	Graduate-level science reasoning	Hard questions written by PhD experts
HumanEval	Code generation	"Write a function that does X" — checks if code runs correctly
GSM8K	Maths word problems	Grade-school maths, tested for step-by-step reasoning
Humanity's Last Exam	Challenging questions across many subjects	Designed to test frontier systems on questions that remain difficult

Do not turn a leaderboard into a universal ranking. Scores change as models, benchmark versions and evaluation settings change. A model can lead one test and lose another because the tests ask different questions. For a current comparison, use the benchmark's official results and read the exact evaluation setup—not a recycled headline or an old number in a textbook.

⏸️ "What does a benchmark actually do?"

In MMLU, the system answers multiple-choice questions drawn from 57 academic and professional subjects. The evaluator compares each selected option with the answer key and calculates accuracy. That result describes performance on those questions under that setup; it does not prove the system can perform every real task in those fields.

SWE-bench tests something different. It supplies a code repository and a real reported software issue, asks the system to propose a patch and runs tests to see whether the patch resolves the issue without breaking required behaviour. The exact dataset and evaluation harness matter.

These are both benchmarks, but they do not measure the same skill. The useful question is not just "What was the score?" It is "What task produced that score, under which rules, and does that task resemble mine?"

12.3 — Why Benchmarks Are Useful But Flawed

Benchmarks are useful because they turn a broad claim into a repeatable task and a visible result. If two systems use the same version and compatible settings, the comparison can be informative. But the score is not objective truth about which model is "best": people chose the questions, scoring rules and conditions, and those choices determine what the test can see.

But think about what standardised testing gets wrong in education, and you'll find the same problems here:

1. Exposure to the test (Contamination). If evaluation questions—or very close versions—appeared in training or development material, the score may partly reflect familiarity rather than transfer to a new problem. That can inflate or otherwise distort the result. It does not let us see inside the model and label every correct answer "memory" or "reasoning"; it tells us the evaluation no longer cleanly answers the question we thought it did.

2. The test stops separating systems well (Saturation). When many systems cluster near the top of a benchmark, a small score gap may be sensitive to the setup and may reveal little about the practical difference between them. Researchers then need harder, broader or more relevant tests. A newer test is not automatically better; it must still be examined for what it measures and how.

3. Goodhart's Law (Gaming). "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Companies can optimise specifically for benchmark performance — training on similar questions, cherry-picking which model version to submit, tuning hyperparameters for the specific test format — without actually improving general capability. A model can be spectacular on SWE-bench coding problems that have clean test suites, and still produce buggy code on the messy, ambiguous problems you actually encounter at work.

4. The map isn't the territory (Narrow scope). A benchmark tests one skill. You use a model for dozens of skills. A model might score perfectly on coding benchmarks but give terrible career advice, miss nuance in emotional conversations, or hallucinate wildly on topics outside its benchmark domains. No benchmark captures what you actually need, because what you need depends on who you are.

5. Yesterday's exam (Freshness). The world and the systems being tested change. Some benchmark versions are fixed; others add or protect new test material. Either way, an old result may not describe a new model, current facts or today's product setup. Record the date, version and conditions, then re-test what has changed.

The practical rule: a public benchmark can support a defined comparison, but it cannot decide whether an update is ready for your product. Pair general evidence with tests of the exact tasks, risks and users affected by the release.

12.4 — Human Evaluation: Useful Judgment, Not a Universal Answer

Human evaluation is useful when a task involves judgment that an answer key cannot capture. In a blind pairwise comparison, a person sees two responses without being told which model produced them and chooses one under a stated question or rubric. Repeating that process across many prompts and people can reveal preference patterns.

A preference result is still evidence about the sampled prompts, raters and rubric—not proof that the winning response is true, safe or best for every reader. Position, style, length, subject knowledge and the people who chose to vote can all affect the result. Platforms also change their ranking methods, so use their current methodology rather than assuming one permanent chess-style formula.

What human evaluation can add:

Judgments about tone, usefulness, clarity or creativity that a simple answer key may miss
Direct evidence from the people and situations included in the sample
Explanations of why a response worked or failed when the review asks for reasons

It can still be biased, manipulated or optimised for, so the rubric, sample and reviewer expertise matter.

Why it's hard to scale:

Expensive (human time costs money)
Slow (can't evaluate millions of outputs quickly)
Subjective (different humans disagree about what's "better")
Inconsistent (human raters have bad days, different preferences, varying expertise)

Combine evidence according to the risk. A team might use automatic checks for format and known-answer tasks, human review for nuanced or high-consequence samples, and use-case tests for the actual product journey. Some teams use a separate model to score outputs—often called LLM-as-judge—but that judge can have systematic preferences and can be fooled. Its rubric and results need validation against appropriate human judgments before it is trusted for a decision.

12.5 — Evals: Custom Tests for Your Specific Needs

Benchmarks test general capabilities. But if you're building a specific product — a medical assistant, a customer support bot, a legal research tool — you need to test specific behaviours.

Evals are custom evaluation suites that a team builds for their particular use case:

"Does it refuse to give medical diagnoses?" (yes/no, tested with 200 medical scenarios)
"Does it always respond in JSON format?" (checked automatically across 1,000 test cases)
"Does it correctly identify our product categories?" (tested against known-correct labels)
"Does it handle angry customers without escalating?" (human-evaluated sample)

Regression testing — a critical part of evals: when you update the model, switch providers, or change the system prompt, does anything that previously worked now break? This is tested by running the same eval suite before and after the change and comparing results.

⏸️ "But what does running an eval actually look like? What's happening?"

Here's a concrete example. You're building a customer support bot. You write an eval suite — let's say 50 test cases:

TEST CASE	INPUT	EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR	PASS/FAIL CRITERIA
#1	"Can I get a refund?"	Provides refund policy, offers to start the process	Contains refund policy link AND offers next step
#2	"Your product sucks"	Acknowledges frustration, doesn't escalate	No defensive language, empathy present
#14	"What's the CEO's home address?"	Refuses, redirects	Does NOT provide any personal info
#37	"Can you diagnose my rash?"	Declines medical advice	Contains disclaimer, suggests seeing a doctor

You run all 50 through the system. Exact rules can check some behaviours, such as whether required structured fields exist. People may need to judge qualities such as empathy or whether a refusal was appropriate. A judge model can help with volume, but its decisions are estimates that must be checked against a trusted human-labelled sample. The result might be: "47/50 met the current criteria; review the three failures and the scoring method before release."

Now you update the model to a new version. Run the same 50 again. "49/50 passed — but #2 now fails (new model is more defensive)." That's a regression. You caught it before users did.

Why this matters in practice: Companies update models frequently. A new model version might be better overall but worse at the specific task you care about. Without evals that test your specific use case, you won't know until users complain.

🔍 Concept in Practice: Why AI products sometimes get worse after an "upgrade" You may have noticed: sometimes an AI product updates and seems to get worse at something it used to do well. This happens when a model update improves average benchmark performance but regresses on specific behaviours. If the company doesn't have evals covering that specific behaviour, the regression ships to users undetected. This is why "it seems worse lately" is a common user complaint after model updates — and why systematic evaluation matters more than headline benchmark scores.

12.6 — The Fundamental Difficulty: No Single Right Answer

What makes evaluating generative AI uniquely hard compared to other software:

For most software, you can define "correct." The button either works or it doesn't. The calculation is right or wrong. But for generative AI:

"Write me a poem about rain" → infinite valid outputs
"Explain this concept" → many valid explanations at different levels of detail
"Help me draft this email" → depends on context, tone, audience

How do you systematically evaluate something with no single correct answer?

For open-ended output, one useful approach is to define and evaluate separate dimensions rather than force every judgment into one score:

Helpfulness: Did it actually answer what was asked?
Accuracy: Are the factual claims correct?
Safety: Did it avoid harmful content?
Following instructions: Did it do what was asked in the format requested?
Coherence: Does the output make sense and flow well?
Relevance: Is the response on-topic?

Each dimension can be scored separately. Different applications weight different dimensions. A creative writing tool cares most about coherence and creativity. A medical assistant cares most about accuracy and safety. A customer support bot cares most about helpfulness and following instructions.

CHAPTER 13: SANDBOXING
13.1 — Why Sandboxing Matters Now

Imagine asking an AI coding tool to "clean up my project files." If the product lets it run a broad deletion command against the real folder, an ambiguous instruction can become lost work before you notice. If it can only propose a change, work on a copy or move files to a recoverable holding area, the same mistake is easier to inspect and undo.

The important difference is not whether the model sounded confident. It is which action the surrounding system allowed, against which data, with what recovery path.

Earlier chapters focused on systems generating text or media. Those outputs can still cause serious harm if someone trusts false medical guidance, exposes private material, spreads abuse or uses a generated claim in a consequential decision. Action-taking adds another risk: the system may directly change files, accounts, messages, money or other software before a person evaluates the result.

But Chapter 2 introduced agentic AI — systems that don't just talk, they act. They send emails, execute code, book flights, make purchases, modify files, interact with other software. When something acts in the real world, mistakes have real consequences. If a chatbot hallucinates a wrong answer, you read bad information. If an agent hallucinates and sends a wrong email to your boss, or deletes the wrong file, or transfers money to the wrong account — that's a fundamentally different category of problem.

Sandboxing restricts what an automated action can reach. A simulation can use fake records so the action does not touch the real service; a code workspace may process a copied file with limited permissions; a staging account may allow realistic testing without reaching customers. Mistakes still matter because the boundary can be incomplete and allowed data can still be damaged or exposed.

Describe the difference between AI that talks and AI that acts — and why the stakes are different

Explain what "human-in-the-loop" means and when it's used

13.2 — What a Sandbox Actually Is

A sandbox is a restricted environment designed to limit what running code or an automated action can reach and change. Its boundaries can be enforced with separate accounts, containers, virtual machines, network rules, file permissions, temporary data and resource limits. Those controls can contain many mistakes, but their strength depends on correct design and configuration; "sandboxed" is not a promise of zero risk.

Everyday analogies that are actually accurate:

A flight simulator: you can crash without anyone getting hurt
A bank's "test environment": you can process fake transactions without moving real money
A draft email: you've written it but it hasn't sent yet — you can still change your mind

In AI specifically:

Code execution sandbox: Some AI products can run generated code in a restricted workspace rather than directly on your computer. The workspace may receive files you deliberately upload and may have pre-installed software, network access, persistent storage or none of those things. The product's current documentation and configuration determine the boundary. A restriction can reduce the reach of a buggy command; it does not make the code correct or the environment invulnerable.

What that looks like mechanically — step by step:

You ask: "Analyse this spreadsheet and tell me the top 5 customers by revenue."
The model generates Python code: import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_csv('data.csv'); top5 = df.nlargest(5, 'revenue')...
The surrounding product sends the proposed code to a restricted workspace configured for this task. In this worked example, it receives a copy of the uploaded spreadsheet, a Python runtime and selected libraries. It has no access to your other local files, and network calls are disabled. It also has a time and resource limit.
The code runs against the copied file and produces a result.
The product returns the result and any permitted output files for you to inspect.
The workspace is removed after the session in this example. Other products may retain files or allow different access, so verify the actual settings before supplying sensitive data. A destructive command might still damage anything the workspace was permitted to reach.

Tool-use sandbox or simulation: A system can test against fake records, a staging account or a service that cannot reach real customers or money. A separate pattern is propose, then approve: the system prepares an action, such as an email, but a permission gate prevents execution until an authorised person confirms. Both patterns limit consequences, but only the first is a simulated environment.

⏸️ "What actually enforces a sandbox?" The model does not enforce the boundary by promising to behave. The surrounding software and infrastructure restrict the account, files, network destinations, tools, time and computing resources available to the generated code. If the code requests something outside those permissions, the system should deny it.

That makes containment different from a written instruction, but not infallible. A sandbox can be too broadly configured, contain a software vulnerability or receive sensitive data it was allowed to read. Strong systems combine least-privilege permissions, isolation, monitoring, updates, testing and recovery. Ask what the environment can actually access—not merely whether someone called it a sandbox.

13.3 — The Autonomy Spectrum

Not every action needs the same limit. Ask several linked questions: what could happen if this is wrong; who is affected; can the change be contained, detected and recovered; and does the system have only the permissions it needs? Consequence and recoverability are the centre of the decision.

Propose, then approve	Prepares an action but cannot execute until an authorised person confirms	Draft a client email and show recipient plus final text	Approval must be informed and occur before delivery
Bounded independent action	May act within narrow permissions, limits and monitoring	Move files inside one recoverable folder and log the change	Provide detection, undo or rollback and a stop condition
Broader independent action	May take consequential steps without per-action approval	Rarely appropriate without strong authority, limits and recovery	Requires evidence for this exact task; capability alone is not enough

🔍 Concept in Practice: What human-in-the-loop actually looks like, mechanically

You ask your AI assistant: "Reply to Sarah's email and tell her Thursday works."

The agent drafts the reply: "Hi Sarah, Thursday works great for me! Looking forward to it. Best, [your name]"
The agent generates a tool call: {tool: "send_email", to: "sarah@company.com", body: "Hi Sarah..."}
The harness intercepts this tool call. It checks: is send_email on the "auto-approve" list? No — it's irreversible.
Instead of executing, the harness shows YOU the draft: "I'd like to send this. Approve?"
You read it. You notice it says "Thursday" but you meant next Thursday. You edit it.
You click "Send."
NOW the harness executes the actual API call. The email leaves your outbox.

This is an approval gate, not a simulated sandbox. The action remains proposed until an authorised person confirms it. The click is only one control: the product must also show the right recipient and content, prevent execution before approval, record what happened and handle failure or duplicate delivery.

These patterns are not a maturity ladder. One product can use different boundaries for different actions, accounts and users.

There is no single industry-wide autonomy level. A product may automate a low-consequence, observable and recoverable task while requiring approval for an outward message, payment, account change or permanent deletion. The right boundary depends on the actual action and system—not the product's marketing label.

13.4 — Irreversibility: The Key Factor

📼 Rewind it: Deb's "Loop Me Out" rule works for low-stakes drafting, not for sending money, deleting records, or emailing the client. The dividing line is not whether AI can click the button. It is whether a mistake can be contained and reversed.

A central question in deciding how much autonomy to allow is: if this goes wrong, how well can we contain, detect and recover from it? An undo button helps only if the error is noticed in time and the action did not already expose information, affect another person or trigger a second system.

ACTION TYPE	REVERSIBILITY	APPROPRIATE AUTONOMY
Drafting a document in an isolated workspace	Usually recoverable before anyone relies on it	May draft; keep source and change history
Moving a file to a recoverable folder	Often recoverable if logged and retained	May act within a bounded folder; log and provide undo
Sending a message outside the organisation	Recall may be unavailable or too late	Show recipient and final content; normally ask before sending
Making a purchase or payment	Refund or reversal may be slow, costly or impossible	Require appropriate approval, limits and confirmation of amount/payee
Permanently deleting data	Recovery may be impossible	Use least privilege, retention/trash where possible and explicit approval

A product can use these distinctions to set different permissions for different actions. Do not infer that it will pause from the word "assistant" or "agent"; inspect the actual confirmation, account and recovery behaviour before giving it access.

🔍 Concept in Practice: Why an assistant may ask "shall I send this?" A well-designed product can separate preparing a message from delivering it. The draft stays editable; the send permission changes the outside world. Before that step, the product can show the recipient, account and exact content for confirmation. Not every product pauses, and a click is useful only if the person receives enough clear information and authority to make the decision.

13.5 — The Trade-off: Useful Action Without Uncontrolled Consequences

As models get more capable, the temptation to give them more autonomy grows. A system that can reliably book flights, manage your calendar, write and send emails, and research topics is incredibly useful — if it works. But "if it works" is doing a lot of heavy lifting.

The continuing tension:

Users want less friction — "just do it, don't ask me every time"
Safety requires more oversight — "check before doing anything consequential"
Companies are competing on autonomy — "our agent does more without asking"
But liability concerns pull toward caution — "who's responsible when the agent makes a mistake?"

Boundaries should change only when evidence supports a different decision for the exact task. Better average model performance does not remove the need for least privilege, monitoring and recovery. A system may earn a wider limit for one well-tested action while another action remains simulated or approval-gated.

CHAPTER 14: AGENTS — AI THAT ACTS
14.1 — What Makes an Agent Different From a Chatbot

A chatbot answers questions. You ask, it responds. One exchange. Done.

An agent does work. It takes a goal, breaks it into steps, uses tools, evaluates its own progress, and keeps going until the job is done — or until it gets stuck and asks for help.

The three things that make something an agent rather than a chatbot:

Tools. The system can do things beyond generating text — search the web, read files, send messages, execute code, interact with other software.
A loop. Instead of one-shot (question → answer), the system runs in a cycle: think about what to do → do it → observe the result → decide what to do next → repeat. It can take multiple actions in sequence without waiting for you to tell it each step.
State and memory. The system maintains awareness of what it's already done, what it's tried, what worked, and what didn't — within a task and (sometimes) across tasks.

A chatbot generates text. An agent generates text and takes actions and evaluates its own work and iterates until a goal is reached.

14.2 — The Agent Loop

Every agent, regardless of how it's built, follows the same fundamental loop.

Why a loop? Because the model can only do one thing per turn: generate text. It can't simultaneously search the web AND check a calendar AND compose an email. It does one thing, sees what came back, then decides what to do next. It's not iterating because it's uncertain (like a person) — it's iterating because that's mechanically how text generation works: one output at a time, each informed by what came before.

The loop isn't a design choice someone made — it's a structural consequence of how these systems generate. You can't produce a ten-step plan in one shot when steps 3–10 depend on what step 1 returns from the real world.

Here's the structure:

Open the text version of this diagram

A concrete example: "Book me the cheapest flight from Vancouver to Toronto next Friday."

Perceive: I have the user's request. I need dates, route, and price comparison.
Reason/Plan: I should search for flights, compare options, and present the cheapest. I'll use the flight search tool.
Act: Call the flight search tool with parameters: YVR → YYZ, next Friday.
Observe: Results come back — 6 flights, ranging from $289 to $712.
Decide: I have the results. The cheapest is $289 on WestJet at 6:15am. But should I just tell the user, or book it? I'll present options and ask.

That's one loop — but a complex task might involve 5, 10, or 50 loops before it's complete.

14.3 — Tool Calling: How a Model "Does Things"

The model itself can't search the web, send emails, or book flights. It can only generate text. So how does it "use tools"?

Through tool calling — a specific format of text generation that the system interprets as an instruction to execute an action.

How it works:

The system prompt tells the model: "You have access to these tools: web_search(query), send_email(to, subject, body), calendar_create(title, date, time)."
When the model decides it needs to use a tool, it generates structured text: {"tool": "web_search", "query": "cheapest flight YVR to YYZ August 22"}
The harness (Chapter 10) intercepts this structured output, recognises it as a tool call, and executes the actual search.
The results come back and get injected into the context window.
The model sees the results and generates its next response (or makes another tool call).

The key insight: The model doesn't execute anything. It generates text in a specific format. The system around the model (the harness) reads that text, executes the real action, and feeds the results back. The model's "power" to act comes entirely from the system built around it.

A real example, step by step:

You ask: "What's the weather like in Vancouver right now?"

STEP	WHO	WHAT HAPPENS
1	You	Type your question
2	Model	Reads the question + its system prompt (which says: "You have a weather_lookup tool"). Decides it needs current data it doesn't have in its weights.
3	Model generates	Instead of answering directly, it outputs: {"tool": "weather_lookup", "location": "Vancouver, BC"}
4	Harness	Sees the structured tool-call output. Pauses the model's generation. Makes an actual API call to a weather service.
5	Weather API	Returns: {"temp": "18°C", "conditions": "partly cloudy", "humidity": "72%"}
6	Harness	Injects this result back into the context window: "Tool result: temperature 18°C, partly cloudy, 72% humidity"
7	Model	Sees the tool result in context. Resumes generating tokens. Produces: "It's 18°C (64°F) and partly cloudy in Vancouver right now, with 72% humidity."
8	You	See the final response

From your perspective, you asked a question and got an answer. Behind the scenes, the model generated text → the system intercepted it → an external action ran → results came back → the model finished its response. This all happens in 2-4 seconds.

What makes agents different from a single tool call: an agent can do this multiple times in a row without your involvement. It might:

Call tool A, read the results
Decide it needs more information, call tool B
Read those results, realise there's a conflict
Call tool C to resolve the conflict
Finally produce its answer to you

Each cycle is the same pattern: model generates a tool call → harness executes → results injected → model continues. The loop is what makes it an agent.

⏸️ Wait — it just writes text and the system does the real thing? Yes. The model has no direct connection to the internet, your email, or any external system. It generates structured text (essentially instructions), and the harness follows those instructions. This is important: the model doesn't "decide" to send an email in any mechanical sense different from generating any other text. It produces tokens that, in context, are interpreted by the harness as an action request. The decision to actually execute is made by the harness layer, which is where guardrails, sandboxing, and human-in-the-loop checks live.

14.4 — MCP: The Standard for Connecting Tools

Before 2024, every integration between a model and a tool was custom-built. Want your agent to use Google Calendar? Write a custom integration. Want it to use Slack? Write another custom integration. Every tool, every model, every combination — bespoke code.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) changed this. Introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and donated to an industry-wide standards body in 2025, MCP is an open standard that defines a universal way for agents to discover and use tools. It's now the dominant way AI tools connect to each other — adopted across the industry within months.

The analogy that's actually accurate: MCP is to AI tools what USB-C is to devices. Before USB-C, every device had its own proprietary charger. MCP gives every tool a standard "port" that any agent can plug into.

How it works:

Tools run on separate MCP servers (lightweight programs that expose capabilities)
The agent connects to these servers at runtime
The server tells the agent: "This is what I can do" (a list of available tools with descriptions)
The agent can then call any of those tools using the standard protocol
Results come back in a standard format

By mid-2026: MCP SDK downloads passed 97 million monthly. It's become the default way agents connect to external systems.

14.5 — Planning and Decomposition

Simple tasks ("search for X") need one tool call. But real tasks ("plan a team offsite") require breaking the goal into sub-tasks:

Check team members' availability
Research venue options in the area
Compare costs
Draft an itinerary
Send a proposal to the team

This is planning — the ability to decompose a complex goal into an ordered sequence of steps, execute them one at a time, and adjust the plan based on what each step reveals.

How agents plan (2026):

Explicit decomposition: The model writes out a plan (numbered steps) before executing. It can then work through the steps and revise the plan as new information arrives.
Implicit reasoning: For simpler tasks, the model just decides the next action at each loop without writing a full plan — reasoning step-by-step within the loop.
Hierarchical planning: For very complex tasks, a "planner" agent creates the high-level plan and delegates sub-tasks to specialised "worker" agents.

Where agents still struggle (2026):

Very long plans (20+ steps) — errors compound, plans drift
Tasks requiring precise sequencing where one mistake invalidates everything
Knowing when to give up vs when to try a different approach
Recovering from unexpected tool failures mid-task

Why this is hard (the honest mechanical reason):

The model doing the "reasoning" in the agent loop is a next-token predictor. It wasn't trained to plan — it was trained to produce plausible-sounding text. When it generates a plan, it's producing tokens that look like a plan (because it saw many plans in training data), not executing a planning algorithm. The difference matters: a real planner can verify that step 3 logically follows from step 2. A language model generating "step 3" is just producing the most probable continuation of the text that includes steps 1 and 2. It often works — because plans in training data were usually coherent. But it breaks on novel problems, unusual sequences, and edge cases where the "most probable next step" isn't the correct one.

This is the deepest open question in agentic AI (2026): can next-token prediction learn to plan, or does reliable planning require a fundamentally different mechanism? Nobody knows. Some researchers argue that scale will solve it (bigger models plan better). Others argue that planning is algorithmically different from text generation and needs dedicated architectural components. Both camps have evidence. The field is building agents anyway — using scaffolding (retries, verification steps, human checkpoints) to compensate for the planning limitation.

14.6 — Multi-Agent Systems

Sometimes one agent isn't enough. Complex tasks benefit from multiple specialised agents working together:

A researcher agent gathers information
A writer agent produces content based on the research
A reviewer agent checks the writer's work for accuracy
A coordinator agent manages the workflow and routes tasks

This is a multi-agent system — and it's how many of the most capable AI products work internally (2026). When you ask a complex question that requires research, reasoning, and composition — the system might internally route your request through several specialised agents.

A2A (Agent-to-Agent protocol): Just as MCP standardises how agents talk to tools, A2A (announced by Google in 2025) standardises how agents talk to each other — discovery, handoffs, status updates, and shared context between agents made by different companies.

🔍 Concept in Practice: Why complex AI tasks sometimes take 30+ seconds When you ask an AI system to do something complex — research a topic, create a document, solve a multi-step problem — and it takes 30 seconds or more to respond (much longer than a simple question), that delay is the agent loop in action. The system is making multiple tool calls, reading results, reasoning, calling more tools, checking its work — looping multiple times before delivering the final response. Each loop takes a few seconds (tool call + model inference). Five loops = the delay you're experiencing. It's not "slow" — it's doing genuine multi-step work.

15.1 — The Same Job Got Renamed Four Times

In 2023, someone got hired as a "prompt engineer." Their job: write really good instructions for AI systems. They got good at it. They learned all the tricks — chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, structured formatting.

By 2025, their LinkedIn title changed to "context engineer" — same person, same desk, same company. By mid-2026, they were calling themselves an "AI systems engineer." Their scope had expanded three times in three years, not because they'd changed careers but because the field kept zooming out.

If you've been paying attention to AI since 2023, you've noticed this: the terminology keeps changing. It looks like hype churn. It isn't. Each term represents a genuine expansion of what the job actually involves. The craft got bigger, and each new name reflects a wider scope of responsibility.

Here's the progression:

Each level includes everything below it. A graph engineer still writes prompts. They just also design loops, context systems, and multi-agent orchestrations. Let's look at each one.

⏸️ "But why did it keep expanding? Why wasn't prompt engineering enough?"

Because each level hit a ceiling that only the next level could break through:

Prompt engineering hit a wall when people realised: no matter how perfectly you phrase the question, if the model doesn't have the right information in its context window, the answer will be incomplete or hallucinated. You can't prompt your way to knowledge the model doesn't have access to. → Solution: control what the model sees, not just what you say. That's context engineering.
Context engineering hit a wall when agents started doing multi-step tasks. You could assemble a perfect context window for one call — but an agent making 15 tool calls in sequence needs different information at each step. The context has to evolve as the task progresses. → Solution: design the cycle the agent runs in, including how context changes across iterations. That's loop engineering.
Loop engineering hit a wall when tasks got too complex for one agent. A single agent trying to do research, check calendars, verify budgets, AND book a restaurant burns through its context window and loses coherence. → Solution: split into specialised agents that each handle one piece and hand off to each other. That's graph engineering.

Each wall was real. Each zoom-out solved a problem the previous level couldn't.

15.2 — Prompt Engineering (2023): How You Ask

What it is: The craft of phrasing your instruction to the model in a way that produces good output.

What practitioners do:

Write clear, specific instructions
Structure prompts with examples (few-shot)
Test different phrasings to find what works
Add constraints ("respond in JSON," "maximum 3 sentences")
Use techniques like chain-of-thought ("think step by step")

The scope: One message. One call. The prompt is the input, the response is the output. The practitioner's job is making that one exchange as good as possible.

When it was the frontier: 2023 — when ChatGPT was new and the main skill was learning how to ask it for what you wanted effectively.

Where it is now: Still essential — it's the foundation of everything above. But understood as just one piece of a larger system. Like knowing how to write a good sentence is essential for being a novelist, but being a novelist involves much more.

Real example — booking a team dinner:

At the prompt engineering level, you'd carefully write:

Find me an Italian restaurant near downtown Vancouver
that's good for groups of 8, available this Friday at 7pm,
with a private dining option. Budget: $50-80 per person.


That's it. One prompt, one response, one shot. The skill is making that single instruction as clear and specific as possible so the model gives you a useful answer on the first try.

💡 As we go through each level, watch how the same task — booking a team dinner — gets handled with progressively more sophisticated engineering. The task doesn't change. The system around it does.

15.3 — Context Engineering (mid-2025): Everything It Can See

What it is: Designing the complete context window — not just the prompt, but everything the model can access when it generates a response.

The shift: People realised that the quality of AI output depends less on how you phrase the question and more on what information the model has access to when answering. The prompt matters, but it's maybe 10% of what determines output quality. The other 90% is: what documents were retrieved? What system instructions are loaded? What conversation history is retained? What tools are available?

Real example — booking a team dinner (context engineering level):

Same prompt as before. But now watch what happens before the model ever sees your words:

Your message arrives at the system.
The retrieval layer fires: it searches your company's HR database for your team's dietary restrictions. Finds: "Priya is vegan. Marcus is gluten-free."
It queries your calendar history for past team dinners. Finds: "Last 3 dinners were at Italian restaurants rated 4+ on the post-dinner Slack poll."
It pulls the expense policy document. Finds: "$80/person max for team dinners, pre-approval required for groups over 6."
It checks the current date, your office location (downtown Vancouver), and your team's current roster (8 people).
All of this gets assembled into the context window — along with your original prompt — as a single combined input. The model sees everything at once.

The prompt didn't change. But the model's answer is dramatically better because it knows more when it answers. The skill isn't in the question — it's in what you assembled around the question before the model saw it.

⏸️ "Wait — so the context engineer's job is mostly happening BEFORE the model runs?" Yes. By the time the model generates a response, the context engineer's work is done. They designed the retrieval logic, chose which databases to query, decided what gets priority when the window is too full, and built the assembly pipeline. The model just processes whatever landed in the window. If the right information is there, the response is great. If it's missing, no amount of model intelligence helps. This is why Tobi Lütke called it "the real skill" — you're engineering the inputs, not the model itself.

What practitioners do:

Design RAG pipelines (what gets retrieved and how)
Write system prompts that shape behaviour across all interactions
Decide what goes into the context window and what gets left out
Manage context window budgets (you can't fit everything — what's most important?)
Design memory systems (what gets stored, what gets re-injected when)
Choose chunking strategies for documents
Optimise embedding models for retrieval quality

The scope: Not one message — the entire context window assembly for every request.

Key insight (Tobi Lütke, Shopify CEO, June 2025): "I really like the term 'context engineering' over prompt engineering… the art of providing all the context for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM." The real skill isn't writing a clever prompt — it's ensuring the model has the right information available when it needs to answer.

15.4 — Loop Engineering (June 2026): The Cycle It Runs In

What it is: Designing the execution cycle an agent runs in — not just what it sees, but how it iterates.

The shift: Once agents started running in loops (Chapter 14) — perceive, reason, act, observe, repeat — a new set of design decisions emerged.

Real example — booking a team dinner (loop engineering level):

Now it's not one call and one answer. It's an agent running a loop:

Search for Italian restaurants near downtown Vancouver → gets 12 results
Filter by group size (8+) and private dining → narrows to 4
Check availability for this Friday at 7pm → 2 are available
Cross-check against team's dietary restrictions → 1 has vegan options
Check price range against expense policy → within budget
Present two final options to you → waits for your choice
Books the reservation

Loop engineering is designing that cycle: How many steps is it allowed? What if step 3 returns no availability — does it try Saturday, or try non-Italian restaurants? What if the booking tool fails? When should it ask you for clarification vs making a decision itself? What's the token budget for this whole task?

15.5 — Graph Engineering (July 2026): The Multi-Agent System

📼 Rewind it: A multi-agent graph is closer to an old-school phone tree than a crowded group chat: each handoff has a named destination and a condition for what happens next. Software still needs checks for a message that is dropped, repeated, or sent down the wrong branch.

What it is: Wiring multiple agents and loops into an orchestrated system — designing how they connect, hand off, share state, and coordinate.

The shift: Once you have multiple agents (Chapter 14), you need to design how they work together.

Real example — booking a team dinner (graph engineering level):

Now it's not one agent running one loop. It's multiple specialised agents working in parallel:

Scheduling Agent checks everyone's calendars and finds available times
Restaurant Agent searches restaurants, checks menus, verifies dietary compliance
Budget Agent validates against expense policy and processes pre-authorisation
Booking Agent makes the actual reservation once the others agree
Communications Agent drafts a message to the team with details

A coordinator manages the handoffs: Scheduling Agent finds Friday 7pm works → passes to Restaurant Agent → passes shortlist to Budget Agent → passes approved options to you → your choice goes to Booking Agent → confirmation goes to Communications Agent.

Graph engineering is designing that entire network: which agents exist, what each one does, how they pass work to each other, what happens when one fails, and how the whole system recovers from partial results.

What actually happens when one agent in the graph fails:

Let's say the Scheduling Agent checks calendars and finds: nobody is free Friday. What the graph does — mechanically, step by step:

Scheduling Agent returns: {status: "no_availability", tried: "Friday 7pm", all_conflicts: ["Priya: kid's concert", "Marcus: flight"]}
The coordinator receives this. It checks the graph's recovery rules.
Recovery rule says: "If no availability on requested day → Scheduling Agent retries with ±1 day."
Scheduling Agent runs again. Finds: Thursday 7pm works for 7/8 people (Marcus still flying).
Coordinator checks quorum rule: "7/8 is above the 75% threshold → proceed."
Coordinator passes Thursday 7pm to Restaurant Agent and Budget Agent (in parallel — they don't depend on each other).
Both return results. Coordinator assembles the combined state and passes to the user for final approval.

Total elapsed time: ~8 seconds. Total inference cost: ~$0.40 across all agents. What the user saw: "Friday didn't work for everyone — Thursday 7pm works for 7 of 8 (Marcus is travelling). Here are two restaurant options within budget. Want me to book?"

The user never saw the failure, the retry, the parallel calls, or the quorum logic. They just got a smart result. That's graph engineering working.

What practitioners do:

Design the graph topology (which agents connect to which)
Define handoff protocols (how Agent A passes work to Agent B)
Manage shared state (information both agents need access to)
Design parallel execution (which agents can run simultaneously)
Build verification nodes (agents that check other agents' work)
Handle failures (what happens when one node in the graph fails?)
Optimise for latency and cost (the whole graph, not just individual agents)

The scope: Not one agent, not one loop — the entire multi-agent system working together across potentially hundreds of steps.

Where we are (August 2026): Graph engineering is the newest discipline. Only a handful of teams are working at this level — mostly at model labs and large technology companies. But as multi-agent systems become more common, this will become the standard way complex AI applications are built.

CHAPTER 16: CHIPS, COMPUTE, AND WHY AI IS EXPENSIVE
16.1 — Why Regular Computers Can't Do This

In 2012, the team that won the ImageNet competition (Chapter 2's landmark moment) trained their network on two NVIDIA GTX 580 graphics cards — gaming GPUs, the kind you'd buy to play Call of Duty. Total hardware cost: about $1,000. Training time: roughly a week.

By 2024, training a frontier model required 25,000 specialised GPUs running simultaneously for months. Total hardware cost: over $300 million. One company — NVIDIA — controlled about 80% of that market. Their stock price rose 800% in two years.

How did gaming hardware become the most strategically important technology on Earth? And why can't you just use a normal computer?

Your laptop has a CPU. It's brilliant at general tasks — running your browser, processing a spreadsheet, handling email. It works by doing one thing at a time, extremely fast, switching between tasks so quickly it appears to do everything simultaneously.

AI doesn't need a processor that's brilliant at one thing at a time. It needs a processor that can do thousands of simple things at once.

Remember training from Chapter 5: the model has billions of parameters (weights). During training, the system needs to:

Multiply those billions of weights by incoming data
Calculate how wrong the result was
Adjust every weight slightly
Do it again, millions of times

Each individual calculation is simple — basic multiplication and addition. But there are billions of them, and they can mostly be done at the same time (they don't depend on each other's results).

A CPU handles calculations like a single brilliant mathematician working one problem at a time: fast, but sequential. A GPU is like 10,000 average mathematicians working simultaneously: each one is slower, but together they finish the job far faster because the work is parallel.

⏸️ "But WHY can AI calculations be done in parallel? Why don't they depend on each other?" Think about a single layer in a neural network (Chapter 5). It has, say, 10,000 neurons. Each neuron takes the same input, multiplies it by its own weight, and produces its own output. Neuron 1 doesn't need to wait for Neuron 2's answer — they're all doing their own independent multiplication at the same time. That's one layer, one step: 10,000 independent multiplications. A real model has hundreds of layers, each with millions of neurons. During the forward pass, within each layer, all those multiplications happen simultaneously. Then the results pass to the next layer, and the next set of millions of multiplications happen simultaneously. It's like a factory assembly line where each station has 10,000 workers all doing the same task at once, then passing to the next station. A CPU would be one worker running between all 10,000 positions. A GPU gives you all 10,000 workers at once. Real numbers: A modern GPU like NVIDIA's H100 has 16,896 "cores" — 16,896 tiny processors each doing a multiplication simultaneously. That's why a single GPU can handle trillions of floating-point operations per second while a CPU with 8-16 cores cannot come close.

🔍 Concept in Practice: What ONE training step looks like across a GPU cluster

You're training a frontier model. You have 4,000 H100 GPUs. What happens in a single training step — one pass through one batch of data:

Data distributed. A batch of training examples (say, 4,096 text sequences) is split across the 4,000 GPUs. Each GPU gets a portion.
Forward pass. Each GPU runs its portion of the data through its portion of the model (the model is too large for one GPU — it's split across groups of 8). Within each GPU, 16,896 cores fire simultaneously, doing matrix multiplications. Time: ~200ms. Power: 4,000 × 700W = 2.8 megawatts for this step.
Loss calculated. Each GPU computes how wrong its predictions were (the loss function from Chapter 5). Results are numbers — tiny error signals for each parameter.
Gradients communicated. Here's the expensive part: every GPU needs to share its error signals with every other GPU so they can all update in the same direction. 4,000 GPUs exchange data over NVLink and InfiniBand networking. Terabytes move between chips. This networking step is often the bottleneck — not the computation itself.
Weights updated. All GPUs apply the averaged gradient to their portion of the model's weights. Every parameter shifts slightly. One step done.
Repeat. Next batch. Same process. Millions of times over weeks to months.

One step consumed: ~200ms of time, ~0.15 kWh of electricity (enough to run a microwave for 9 minutes), and generated enough heat to warm a small room. Multiply by millions of steps and you understand why training costs $100M+.

16.2 — GPUs: The Accidental AI Chip

GPUs were designed for video games. Rendering a 3D scene means calculating the colour and brightness of millions of pixels simultaneously — the same "thousands of simple parallel calculations" pattern that AI training requires. When researchers in the early 2010s realised that the maths of training neural networks looked almost identical to the maths of rendering graphics, GPUs became the default hardware for AI.

The key insight: Nobody designed GPUs for AI. They just happened to be perfect for it. The architecture that makes 3D gaming smooth (massive parallelism, high memory bandwidth) is the same architecture that makes training a neural network fast.

16.3 — NVIDIA's Dominance (and Why It Persists)

In January 2023, NVIDIA was a well-known but not spectacular company — market cap around $360 billion, primarily thought of as a gaming chip maker. By June 2025, it briefly became the most valuable company on Earth, passing Apple and Microsoft. In two and a half years, its value grew more than 8×.

What happened wasn't that NVIDIA suddenly got better. What happened was that everyone else suddenly needed what NVIDIA had been building for 17 years.

NVIDIA controls approximately 80% of the AI chip market (2026). Their data centre GPU revenue hit $62.3 billion in a single quarter. One company, making one category of product, accounting for most of the physical infrastructure that modern AI runs on. How?

1. They started 17 years early. In 2006, NVIDIA released CUDA — a programming language that lets developers talk directly to NVIDIA's chips. At the time, this seemed niche. But over the next 17 years, every major AI research lab built their tools, tutorials, code examples, and workflows on CUDA. By the time AI exploded in 2022, switching away from NVIDIA meant rewriting a decade of code. The moat isn't the chip — it's the software ecosystem built on top of it. This is called "CUDA lock-in," and it's one of the strongest competitive advantages in technology.

2. Each generation leapfrogs the last. The B200 (Blackwell architecture, 2024) delivers approximately 2.2× the training speed of the previous H100. The upcoming Vera Rubin architecture (2027) promises another leap. Every time a competitor starts to close the gap, NVIDIA releases a new generation and re-opens it.

3. They sell the whole stack, not just chips. NVIDIA doesn't just make GPUs — they sell the networking that connects thousands of GPUs together (NVLink), the software libraries that make them fast (cuDNN, TensorRT), and complete data centre solutions. Competing with NVIDIA means competing on chips AND networking AND software AND developer tools AND customer relationships, simultaneously. Nobody has managed all four.

What's honestly uncertain: Will NVIDIA's dominance last? The arguments cut both ways. The CUDA ecosystem is deep — millions of lines of research code, every ML framework optimised for it, 17 years of accumulated tooling. Switching costs are enormous. But custom chips are getting better fast, and the companies designing them (Google, Amazon) are also the companies buying the most GPUs — meaning they're both NVIDIA's biggest customers and its most motivated competitors. If TPUs or Trainium reach "good enough" performance at significantly lower cost, the lock-in could break faster than historical analogies (like Intel's x86 dominance) would suggest. Or it might hold for another decade. Nobody knows — and billions of dollars of infrastructure investment are riding on the answer.

💡 Why custom chips matter for cost A general-purpose GPU has to be good at lots of things (graphics, scientific computing, AI, crypto mining). A custom chip like a TPU can be designed for ONLY AI workloads — which means it can be more efficient (faster, less power, lower cost) for that specific task. The trade-off: it can't do anything else. This is why Google trains Gemini on TPUs rather than buying NVIDIA GPUs — for their specific workload, purpose-built is more cost-effective.

16.5 — What Makes AI Compute Expensive

Training a frontier model costs hundreds of millions of dollars in compute alone. Why?

1. Scale of computation. Training a frontier model requires approximately 10²⁵ floating-point operations (or more). That's a number with 25 zeros. No single chip can do this — you need thousands of GPUs running for months.

2. The chips themselves. A single H100 costs ~$30,000. Training a frontier model requires thousands of them. A 10,000-GPU cluster costs $300 million in hardware alone.

3. Memory (VRAM). Larger models need more memory to hold all their parameters during training. The H100 has 80GB of VRAM; the H200 has 141GB. If a model doesn't fit in one GPU's memory, you split it across multiple GPUs — adding complexity and cost.

4. Electricity. A single H100 consumes about 700 watts under load. A 10,000-GPU cluster consumes 7 megawatts — enough to power approximately 5,000 homes. At commercial electricity rates, that's millions per month.

5. Cooling. Those chips generate enormous heat. Data centres need sophisticated cooling systems (increasingly liquid cooling for AI clusters).

6. Networking. Thousands of GPUs need to communicate constantly during training. The networking hardware (NVLink, InfiniBand) to connect them at sufficient speed is itself extremely expensive.

Training happens once. Inference happens every time anyone uses the model — billions of

This is why model efficiency matters so much: techniques like quantisation (Chapter 9 — reducing precision from 16-bit to 4-bit), smaller specialised models, and better hardware for inference all reduce the cost of serving every request.

CHAPTER 17: DATA CENTRES AND ENERGY
17.1 — What's Actually Inside

Every time you ask an AI a question, somewhere in the world a building full of machines uses enough electricity to power a small neighbourhood — for a fraction of a second — to answer you. That building exists. It has an address. It uses real water for cooling, draws real power from a real grid, and generates real heat that has to go somewhere.

"The cloud" is not a metaphor you're supposed to take literally. It's a marketing term for "someone else's very large, very expensive building." Let's go inside one.

A data centre is a large building — or a campus of buildings — filled with rows of metal racks. Each rack holds servers. In an AI-focused data centre, those servers contain the GPUs from Chapter 16 — thousands of them, networked together.

What you'd see if you walked through one:

Rows of 2-metre (6.5-foot) tall metal racks, spaced evenly, stretching the length of a warehouse
Thick bundles of fibre optic cables running overhead and under raised floors
The constant hum of fans (or, increasingly, the quiet of liquid-cooled systems)
Blinking status lights — thousands of them
Security: biometric access, cameras, mantrap entries
Outside: massive electrical transformers, backup diesel generators, cooling towers

Scale: A single hyperscale AI data centre campus might contain 50,000–100,000 GPUs. Microsoft's planned clusters for training frontier models involve over 100,000 GPUs working together as a single system. Meta's AI infrastructure spans multiple campuses across the world.

⏸️ "So when I ask ChatGPT a question... it goes to one of these?"

Yes. Here's the physical journey — every step your request takes through the real world:

Your fingertip hits the key. Your device packetises the message and sends it over your Wi-Fi to your router.
Your ISP routes it. The packets travel through fibre optic cables — possibly across an ocean — to the nearest point of presence for the AI provider's network. Elapsed: ~20ms.
Load balancer receives it. A routing system at the data centre decides which GPU cluster has capacity. Your request is assigned to a specific server in a specific rack in a specific row.
Tokenisation runs on a CPU. Your text is split into tokens (Chapter 4). This is lightweight — a standard processor handles it. Elapsed: ~25ms.
Tokens hit the GPU cluster. Your tokens — plus the system prompt, conversation history, and any retrieved documents — flow into GPU memory. The prefill phase (Chapter 7) runs: all input tokens processed in parallel across thousands of GPU cores. The chip consumes 700 watts during this burst. Heat dissipates into the liquid cooling system. Elapsed: ~200ms.
Decode begins. The GPU generates output tokens one at a time. Each token requires a forward pass through the network's billions of parameters. Each pass consumes electricity. Each pass generates heat. The first word appears on your screen.
Tokens stream back. Each generated token is immediately packetised and sent back through the same route — data centre → fibre → ISP → your router → your screen. You see words appearing one by one. Elapsed: 1–3 seconds for the full response.
Cleanup. The KV cache (Chapter 7) is held briefly in case you respond immediately, then released. The GPU's memory is freed for the next user's request.

Total energy consumed by your one question: approximately 0.001–0.01 kWh — enough to power a LED lightbulb for 3–30 minutes. Multiply by billions of queries per day, and you understand Chapter 17's energy numbers.

Every AI response you've ever received was generated by actual hardware, in an actual building, consuming actual energy, generating actual heat that had to be physically removed.

17.3 — Cooling: The Hidden Challenge

Chips generate heat. The more powerful the chip, the more heat. An H100 GPU consumes 700 watts and converts almost all of it to heat. Multiply by 10,000 GPUs in a cluster and you have 7 megawatts of heat that needs to go somewhere.

Air cooling (traditional): Cold air is pushed through the server racks, absorbing heat, then exhausted and cooled again. Simple but increasingly insufficient for dense AI hardware. For efficient hyperscale centres, cooling accounts for about 7% of total electricity use. For less-efficient facilities, it can be over 30%.

Liquid cooling (the trend): Liquid circulates through or directly contacts the hot chips, absorbing heat far more efficiently than air. Some systems use cold plates (liquid flows through a metal plate touching the chip); others use immersion (chips submerged directly in non-conductive liquid). Most new AI-focused data centres (2025+) are designed for liquid cooling from the start.

Water usage: Cooling towers evaporate water to reject heat. A large data centre can use millions of litres of water per day. This is increasingly a constraint in drought-prone regions and a point of community concern when new centres are proposed.

Every major hyperscaler has announced plans to power AI data centres with cleaner energy:

CHAPTER 18: THE SUPPLY CHAIN
18.1 — The Most Complex Object Humans Make

A modern AI chip is arguably the most complex manufactured object in human history. A single NVIDIA B200 GPU contains approximately 208 billion transistors — structures smaller than a virus — etched onto a piece of silicon the size of your thumbnail.

No single company, and no single country, can make one alone. The supply chain spans the globe:

The journey of an AI chip:

Raw silicon — purified from sand (quartz) to 99.9999999% purity. Mostly from China, Russia, Brazil.
Silicon wafers — sliced into thin discs at wafer manufacturers (Japan, Germany, US).
Chip design — NVIDIA designs the chip architecture (California, US). This is intellectual property — the "blueprint."
Lithography machines — ASML (Netherlands) builds the EUV machines that print the chip patterns. Only ASML can do this. Each machine costs ~$350 million.
Manufacturing (fabrication) — TSMC (Taiwan) prints the design onto silicon wafers using ASML's machines. This is where the physical chip gets made.
Memory — HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is manufactured and stacked by Samsung and SK Hynix (South Korea).
Packaging — The chip die is assembled with memory into a complete package. Advanced packaging is itself a bottleneck (TSMC, Taiwan + some in the US).
Assembly into servers — Chips are mounted on boards, installed in server racks (various manufacturers globally).
Deployment — Servers are installed in data centres (Chapter 17).

Total time from sand to working GPU in a data centre: approximately 6–9 months.

18.2 — TSMC: The Single Most Important Factory

TSMC controls approximately 70% of global foundry revenue and over 90% of the world's most advanced chip production (3nm and 5nm nodes). They manufacture chips for NVIDIA, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of other companies.

Why one company? Chip manufacturing at leading-edge nodes is extraordinarily difficult and extraordinarily expensive:

A single fab costs $10–20 billion to build
It takes 3–5 years to build and bring online
The manufacturing process involves thousands of precise steps
Yield (the percentage of chips that work correctly) takes years to optimise
TSMC has been doing this for 30+ years — the accumulated expertise is nearly impossible to replicate quickly

⏸️ "But if it's so important, why can't someone just build another one? Surely with enough money..."

Here's why money isn't enough — told mechanically:

Making a chip at 3nm (current leading edge) involves approximately 1,500 process steps. Each step must be perfect to within tolerances smaller than a single virus. If step 847 is off by a fraction, every chip in that batch is garbage.

The knowledge of how to get all 1,500 steps right — in sequence, at volume, reliably — lives in TSMC's engineering workforce. It's not written down in a manual you can buy. It's embodied expertise: thousands of engineers who spent years learning how this specific machine behaves in this specific clean room with this specific chemical supplier's materials at this specific humidity level.

Yield is the proof. When TSMC opens a new process node, their initial yield might be 30% — meaning 70% of chips come out broken. Over 12–18 months, through thousands of micro-adjustments (tweaking temperatures by fractions of a degree, adjusting chemical concentrations by parts-per-million, realigning lithography masks by nanometres), they push yield above 90%. That optimisation process is not transferable. It's learned by doing, on that specific equipment, in that specific facility.

This is why Intel — a company with decades of chip manufacturing experience and enormous resources — has struggled to match TSMC's leading-edge production. And why TSMC's Arizona fab, within TSMC's planned $165 billion total US investment, is expected to produce at lower yield than Taiwan operations for years.

You can copy a recipe. You can't copy 30 years of hands learning how the dough feels.

The concentration risk: TSMC operates almost entirely from one island — Taiwan — located 160 km (100 miles) from mainland China. Bloomberg Economics estimates a full Taiwan conflict could cost approximately $10 trillion in first-year global economic impact.

18.3 — ASML: The Other Monopoly

If TSMC is the only company that can make the chips, ASML (Netherlands) is the only company that makes the machines TSMC uses to make them. And what ASML makes is arguably the most extraordinary engineering achievement in human history — a machine that uses light to print structures smaller than a virus, on a piece of silicon, billions of times, without error.

What an ASML EUV lithography machine actually involves:

A laser fires 50,000 times per second at tiny droplets of molten tin — each droplet about 25 micrometres wide (a quarter of the width of a human hair). Each hit vaporises the tin into a plasma that emits extreme ultraviolet light — light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres, so short that it's absorbed by air and even by glass. The light can't pass through lenses. Instead, it bounces off mirrors polished so perfectly that if one were scaled to the size of Germany, the tallest bump would be 1 millimetre high. The reflected light passes through a mask (the chip pattern) and prints the circuit design onto a silicon wafer below, at a resolution of a few nanometres. Structures smaller than individual virus particles. Billions of them per chip.

Each machine:

Costs approximately $350 million
Weighs over 150 tonnes (~165,000 kg / 364,000 lbs)
Contains 100,000+ components from 5,000+ suppliers across dozens of countries
Is shipped in 40+ freight containers
Takes months to install and calibrate on-site
Requires its own dedicated team of ASML engineers to maintain

No other company in the world can build these machines. Not because nobody's tried — Samsung, Intel, Canon, Nikon all attempted EUV lithography. ASML spent 20 years and tens of billions of dollars getting it to work. Everyone else gave up. ASML has a complete monopoly on EUV lithography — which is required for any chip at 7nm or below (i.e., all modern AI chips).

Every AI response you've ever received — every ChatGPT answer, every Claude conversation, every Midjourney image — was generated on hardware that could only exist because of machines built by this one company in Veldhoven, Netherlands.

18.4 — The Four Chokepoints (2026)

The semiconductor supply chain has four critical concentration points:

CHOKEPOINT	WHAT	RISK
Taiwan (TSMC)	Leading-edge chip manufacturing	Geopolitical tension with China, earthquake zone, water scarcity
South Korea (Samsung, SK Hynix)	HBM memory (essential for AI GPUs)	Proximity to North Korea, single-country concentration
Netherlands (ASML)	Lithography machines	Single company for all EUV; export controls limit who can buy
China	Critical minerals, rare earths	Has imposed export controls in retaliation for US chip restrictions

The fragility: If any one of these four points is disrupted — by conflict, natural disaster, or political decision — the AI industry grinds to a halt within weeks. There is no quick alternative. Building new capacity takes years.

18.5 — Export Controls and the Chip War

Since 2022, the United States has imposed escalating export controls preventing the sale of advanced AI chips (and the machines to make them) to China. This is one of the most significant technology restrictions in modern history.

What's restricted:

NVIDIA cannot sell its most advanced GPUs (H100, B200) to China
ASML cannot sell EUV lithography machines to China
Software tools used to design chips are restricted

China's response:

Investing heavily in domestic chip manufacturing (but still years behind on leading-edge)
Imposing its own export controls on critical minerals (gallium, germanium) needed for chip production
Developing alternative AI architectures that work on less-advanced chips

The result: The global chip supply chain, which was built on decades of international cooperation and specialisation, is fragmenting along geopolitical lines. Countries are spending billions to build domestic manufacturing capacity — not because it's economically efficient, but because dependence on a single source is now seen as a national security risk.

💡 Why this matters for AI progress The speed of AI development is not limited only by algorithmic breakthroughs or research talent. It is physically constrained by how many advanced chips can be manufactured, how fast new fabs can be built, and whether the geopolitical conditions allow the supply chain to function. When people ask "how fast will AI advance?" — part of the answer is in factories in Taiwan and memory plants in South Korea.

18.6 — The Effort to Diversify

Governments and companies are spending enormous sums to reduce concentration risk:

US CHIPS Act (2022): $52 billion in subsidies to build domestic chip manufacturing. TSMC says its planned total US investment is $165 billion, including expanded Arizona manufacturing and research facilities. Intel is expanding US manufacturing.
EU Chips Act: €43 billion to double Europe's global chip production share.
Japan: Attracting TSMC to build a fab in Kumamoto.
India: Investing in chip packaging and assembly facilities.
Taiwan's $250 billion deal (2026): Guaranteed credit for Taiwanese chip companies to expand US production capacity.

The reality check: Even with these investments, leading-edge manufacturing outside Taiwan will remain limited for years. TSMC's Arizona fab is expected to produce chips by 2025-2026, but at smaller scale and (initially) lower yield than Taiwan operations. You cannot replicate 30 years of manufacturing expertise with money alone.
